text: That star you're looking at flew 8.6 years to reach you.
Something wrecked it in the last millisecond.
What?
Don't look at me.
I'm perfectly steady.
Stars don't twinkle.
Not one.
The twinkle happens in about a hundred kilometers of air above your head.
Warm and cold pockets bend light differently,
like shimmer over a hot road.
A star is so far away, its light arrives as one tiny point.
So every air pocket shoves that point around, brighter, dimmer, left, right.
But planets? Much closer. A tiny disk, not a point.
Twinkle? Sorry, I don't do that.
Steady light? Probably a planet. Free tip.
So how do astronomers get the twinkle out?
They climb above as much air as they can.
Chile's Atacama, one of Earth's driest deserts, telescopes 2,600 meters up.
India chose Hanli in Ladakh, 4,500 meters, now India's first dark-sky reserve.
Europe's new 39-meter telescope will bend its mirror about a thousand times a second.
And NASA just left. Hubble orbits about 480 kilometers up. No air, no twinkle.
So every twinkle you ever wished on was our air, not the star.
8.6 years of travel, ruined by a breeze.
Next time a star twinkles, remember, it was steady the whole way.
